newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE- International custody cases not child's play in Egypt.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE- International custody cases not child's play in Egypt.

text.p: Every day, two-year-old Lisa Bachir frolics in the rooftop wading pool or spacious palm gardens at the French ambassador's residence in Egypt.

Surrounded by a high wall embracing the villa and embassy, the child and her French mother Marie-Laure Iacazzi have been living at the compound since February for security reasons, entangled in a sticky custody case with Lisa's Egyptian father.

"I call on President Hosni Mubarak and the foreign minister to return to me my daughter, who is being held in the French embassy which is disregarding Egyptian law," said a banner raised by Lisa's father, Taha Bachir, during a recent street protest.

The Iacazzi-Bachir case is one of at least 14 international custody disputes which Egypt's Justice Ministry has been trying to resolve between January 1996 and July this year, said judge Sherif Adlam.
The case reached the highest levels of government in June as part of talks in Paris between Mubarak and French President Jacques Chirac.

Legal sources say it also highlights the difficulties of negotiating the social and religious minefields which can plague such highly charged disputes in Egypt, which has not signed the Hague Convention used to resolve international custody.
EGYPT SEES BILATERAL TREATIES WORKING WELL
With no specific directives in Egypt on child custody, most countries carve their own path to help their nationals resolve who gets the children after divorce or separation.
"This is why we have bilateral treaties, which work well," said Adlam, referring to Egypt's civil procedure accords with 13 countries.
In the European Union, only France and Italy have such an accord. France's accord with Egypt aims to ensure they carry out the others' judgments and includes articles on child custody.
Italy's civil accord cannot be applied in cases which exceed the constitutional custody age of five or requirements of public order, said Marco Del Panta of the Italian embassy.

"We had a case in which the children were taken away from the Italian mother, who was Christian, by the Egyptian father, a Moslem. We settled with the cooperation of the Egyptian government, who recognised her right to see the children.
"For the moment it's a satisfactory compromise."
CLASH OF CULTURES
Canada is working on an accord to resolve custody issues likely to be in the form of a consular agreement.

"There are very sensitive questions involved, as far as Egypt is concerned, dealing with Islam and different perceptions of the role of the mother and father," said a Canadian official. "We're trying to manage these issues as best as we can."
Diplomats doubt that a judicial accord solves any problems.
"I don't think it's worth the paper it's printed on," said one. "We get a lot of help informally. But I'm talking about access. Getting children back you could never work informally."
The French-Egyptian treaty says the child should be returned to the country of residence and for both countries to implement judgements as long as they do not contravene public order.
While clear in letter, the matter can be complicated in reality, especially when public order has religious overtones.
The Egyptian media has reported Bachir's view that he is being denied access. "The Tragedy of Marriage to Foreigners," said Al-Akhbar. "The embassy refuses to implement Egypt's law..."
"When God gave them a daughter, the mother called her Lisa, refusing categorically to call her (the Moslem name) Fatima," said another newspaper. "That's when the problems started."
"It is a problem related to the sociology of mixed marriage in general," said lawyer Yassin Tageldin.

"The (Bachir) family is trying to place all these problems on the grounds of religion, saying that Marie-Laure is trying to baptise Lisa and to bring her up as a Christian, and she should be brought up as a Moslem."
DIFFERENT COURT RULINGS COMPLICATE CASE
He said the case started when a French court gave Iacazzi custody after Bachir took Lisa to Egypt and the couple separated in 1996. Two Egyptian courts later upheld the custody decision.

Many expected the Iacazzi custody ruling to be implemented in Egypt because of the bilateral accord. But a third Egyptian court said Bachir was not notified and overturned the rulings, prompting France's justice ministry to protest.

After each court ruling Iacazzi tried to leave Egypt with Lisa. But immigration officials turned them back and once took them off the plane, partly because they needed Bachir's permission to travel, diplomats and legal sources said.
Bachir's family has sought intervention from high quarters.

In a letter to the foreign minister obtained by Reuters, Taha Bachir's father asked for help to prevent them leaving Egypt "for the sake of my granddaughter's religion, which is a point of difference between my son and his French wife. This is a humanitarian appeal for all Egyptians".
In response to another appeal, the interior ministry assured Bachir he had the right to see his daughter whenever he wanted.
Adlam said that when the court returns after the summer, he expects the case to be solved objectively despite the fact that "the husband says it is not in public order or Islam".
Other custody cases end smoothly. The opposition Al-Wafd newspaper reported that an Egyptian man gave his Belgian wife and daughter permission to leave Egypt, but she decided to stay.
Diplomats emphasise the highly charged custody issues are not confined to Moslem-Christian marriages, and that the Egyptian government is keen to cooperate.
"Our biggest number of custody problems are between Canada and the United States," said one diplomat.
